Heavier panting and noisy breathing are signs of heatstroke. Overheating can damage organs within minutes. Flat-faced and thick-coated breeds are most at risk.

What to do now:
- Move them out of the sun right away, into shade or an air-conditioned room.
- Wet the coat with cool tap water, especially the belly, armpits, groin and paws, then fan them so the water evaporates.
- Offer small sips of cool water if they're alert. Don't force them to drink.
- Keep cooling for 10 to 15 minutes, then go to the vet with the car's air-con on, even if they seem better. Damage can show up hours later.
- If you have a rectal thermometer, stop active cooling at about 39.5 °C so they don't get too cold.

Don't:
- Use ice or ice-cold water. It narrows blood vessels and slows cooling.
- Leave a wet towel draped over them. It traps heat. Wet the coat and keep air moving instead. Waiting to see if they recover on their own.

Go to a vet now.

If your cat does act unwell or has unusual symptoms, move them to a cooler place and go to a vet now.

Benefits include:
- No heat cycles and no unplanned litters
- Lower risk of womb infections and breast tumors in females
- No testicular cancer in males, and less roaming and urine marking

Your vet will decide when to start. Ask your vet, but generally start early.
